cost.headline: Ask suppliers first, pay for site audits only later
cost.summary: The company uses cheap paperwork steps through its existing battery suppliers to find out which refiners are really in its chain. It holds off on paying for its own mine audits until that mapping shows which sites matter.

actions.text: Send every current battery supplier a short questionnaire asking them to name, in writing, the cobalt refiners they use.
Start a risk register that labels every claim as documented, indicator, inference or missing, so no screening flag is ever described as proof of abuse.
Accept refiners' existing independent responsible-sourcing audits instead of paying for new ones, and list the refiners that have none.
Ask named refiners and suppliers for any water, tailings and emissions monitoring they already hold, rather than commissioning new tests.
Pay for independent site checks only at refiners or mines that the mapping actually links to the company's batteries.

cost.tradeoffs: This is the cheapest route, but it relies on what suppliers choose to tell us and on audits someone else designed. Real conditions at sites like TFM stay unchecked for a long time.
cost.commercial: Illustrative assumption: costs are mostly staff time and contract wording, so spending stays low. Illustrative assumption: some suppliers may push back or be slow, which costs time rather than money.
cost.residual_risk: If suppliers give incomplete or wrong refiner names, the company could believe its chain is mapped when it is not. Mixing of industrial and hand-dug cobalt stays unproven either way.

speed.headline: Keep batteries flowing, add the new rules at renewal
speed.summary: The company keeps buying from its current suppliers without pausing deliveries, and adds disclosure and evidence rules each time a contract comes up for renewal. Because Congo's export quotas already squeeze supply, it avoids anything that would cause a sudden supply gap.

actions.text: Ask current suppliers to name their cobalt refiners without making the answer a condition of current orders.
Build Congo's export quotas into the sourcing plan and require any backup supplier to pass the same checks as existing ones.
At each renewal, add clauses that require named refiners and chain-of-custody records.
At each renewal, ask for independent water, tailings and emissions data from the refiner and, where known, the mine.
Add a contract clause saying that if child or forced labour is found, the supplier must fix it with us instead of being dropped overnight.

speed.tradeoffs: Deliveries stay safe, but progress on evidence moves only as fast as the renewal calendar. Contracts that renew late leave gaps open the longest.
speed.commercial: Illustrative assumption: no extra supply disruption, since no supplier is cut off and no order is held up. Illustrative assumption: renewal talks may take somewhat longer as new clauses are negotiated.
speed.residual_risk: For contracts that are not up for renewal soon, the company may go a long time without knowing its refiners. A rushed switch to backup supply under quota pressure could still bring in unchecked refiners if the checks are skipped.

responsible.headline: Prove the chain on a fixed timeline, then fix problems
responsible.summary: The company requires named refiners, chain-of-custody records and independent audits by set deadlines, and uses the results to choose where to send independent labour and environmental checks. If problems are found, it works with suppliers to fix them and help affected people rather than walking away.

actions.text: Require every battery supplier to name its cobalt refiners and provide chain-of-custody records by a fixed deadline.
State openly, inside the company and in public reports, that the environmental picture is blank, and make no green or low-impact claims.
Require each named refiner to show an independent audit based on ILO child-labour and forced-labour standards, with a deadline for those that have none.
Make independent water, tailings and emissions data from the mine and refiner a condition at each contract renewal.
Fund independent labour checks, with private worker interviews and a safe reporting channel, at every mine or route the mapping shows, including TFM and any non-IXM routes if they appear.
If abuse is found, fund a fix plan with the supplier, including help getting affected children into school, instead of quietly dropping the supplier.

responsible.tradeoffs: This costs the most and takes the longest, and some suppliers may refuse or fail the deadlines. It is the only strategy that could eventually show whether the company's cobalt is kept apart from risky hand-dug mines.
responsible.commercial: Illustrative assumption: audit and monitoring costs are clearly higher than the other two strategies. Illustrative assumption: tying hard conditions to renewals rather than current orders limits the risk of a supply gap under the quotas.
responsible.residual_risk: Audits are snapshots and can miss problems, especially at hand-dug sites that inspectors rarely visit. Even a full map would still depend on chain-of-custody records being honest.

resolution: Procurement is right that the company should map its own refiners before paying for audits at TFM, because nothing yet links TFM to its batteries (M2), and Human Rights is right that audits must happen rather than be put off forever. So mapping comes first on a fixed deadline, and any mine or route it turns up, TFM included, automatically gets an independent labour check with private worker interviews.
unresolved: After the trader, nobody knows which refiner handles TFM's cobalt, and no strategy can fix that until suppliers disclose it (M1, I2).
No strategy can yet show that the company's cobalt is kept apart from hand-dug mines, because traders and refiners can mix material from many sources (I3, K3).
Records disagree on who owns TFM, and the reported Gécamines stake comes only from a secondary source (M3, I4).
There is no measured environmental data for the mine or any refiner, so pollution and emissions risk is completely unknown (M4).
Congo's export quotas through 2027 could push buyers toward unchecked refiners if due-diligence checks are rushed or skipped (D3).
verification_needed: Written refiner names and chain-of-custody records from each battery supplier showing which refiner processed the cobalt and whether it was kept separate.
An official registry extract for TFM to settle who actually owns the mine.
Independent site-level labour audits with private worker interviews at any mine or refiner the mapping links to the company's batteries.
Independent, measured water-quality, tailings-dam and emissions data for the mine and the named refiner.
Greenhouse gas figures per tonne of cobalt for each step of the chain: mine, shipping and refining.

messages.text: Three paths: cost (supplier paperwork first), speed (new rules at each renewal so deliveries never stop), and responsible (proof on a fixed timeline, then targeted audits and fixes). None of them lets us claim TFM cobalt is in our batteries, because no evidence shows that yet (M2).

On audits, map our refiners first on a firm deadline, then automatically send independent labour checks to every site that shows up, TFM included. Screening flags call for checks but are never treated as proof of abuse (K1, K2).
